questions.q: Why does a mapping document need to reference a target field's API name rather than just its display label?
options: API names are shorter and easier to type
Salesforce does not allow field labels to appear in any document
Labels can be renamed without changing the underlying field the load actually references, so the API name is what the load tool truly needs
Display labels are not visible to anyone outside the admin team
questions.explain: A field's label can be renamed in Setup without changing its underlying API name — the mapping document has to reference the API name since that's what the load tool actually uses to place data.

questions.q: A legacy "State" field is free text, but the target Salesforce field is a strict picklist. What does this lesson say has to happen before the load?
options: An explicit picklist value translation table has to be built, mapping every known source value to a valid target value with a documented fallback
Nothing — Salesforce automatically converts free text into the closest picklist value
The target field should be changed to free text to avoid the mismatch entirely
The records should simply be excluded from the load without further analysis
questions.explain: Type mismatches like free text into a strict picklist have to be resolved explicitly in the mapping document via a picklist value translation table, built once during design rather than guessed at record by record.

questions.q: Which of these is explicitly listed in this lesson as something a usable mapping document should capture for each field?
options: The Bulk API job Id that will eventually process the load
Whether the target field is required
The name of the sandbox used for rehearsal
The exact time of day the load will run
questions.explain: A usable mapping document captures the source field, the target field's API name, both fields' data types, whether the target is required, and any applicable transformation rule — not load scheduling or environment details.

questions.q: What is the key difference between scope sign-off (Lesson 4) and mapping sign-off, according to this lesson?
options: There is no real difference; both answer the same question
Mapping sign-off only applies to phased migrations, not big-bang ones
Scope sign-off happens after mapping sign-off, not before
Scope sign-off answers whether the right data is being moved; mapping sign-off answers whether it's moving to exactly the right place and in the right way
questions.explain: Scope sign-off is a business decision about which data should move. Mapping sign-off is a more technical review checking that the mapping document correctly and precisely routes that data field by field.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a mapping error caught during mapping sign-off is cheaper than the same error caught during validation in Chapter 3?
options: Because validation errors are always impossible to fix
Because mapping sign-off happens after the load is already complete
Because catching it in review is a quick document edit, while catching it during validation may mean re-running part of a load
Because Chapter 3's validation step cannot detect mapping errors at all
questions.explain: An error caught during line-by-line mapping review is a cheap, early edit. The same error surviving into validation means data has already loaded incorrectly, requiring rework instead of a document fix.
